::: {.callout-tip title="In short"}
- **The idea.** In 2016 the most confident forecast in medicine said
  radiology would disappear. It failed because it mistook a task for a job.
  Four questions (tasks, generalization, liability, demand) let you judge any
  forecast about your own specialty.
- **What you do.** Ask ChatGPT Edu to apply the four questions to your
  specialty and find studies of how its working day is spent, then check one
  in PubMed. Look up how much of each health job people were seen doing
  with one AI company's chatbot.
- **What you keep.** A three-line forecast for your specialty, with a number
  and its source, to reread at the end of residency.
- **Short on time?** Read "What actually happened" and "Why 'he was just
  early' is not enough". Do Part A.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

1. Say what was predicted for radiology in 2016, what the original data (match
   tables and workforce studies) show happened through 2026, and why "he was
   just early" is not a good enough explanation.
2. Ask four questions of the specialty you are entering. Does the job break
   into tasks? Does the tool work outside the hospital that built it? Who is
   liable? Does demand grow? Then use the same questions to check a
   chatbot's forecast about that specialty.
3. Use the story of computer-aided detection in mammography to explain why
   a tool being adopted and a tool improving outcomes are separate questions.
4. Explain why a tool can cut work inside one hospital while raising cost
   across the whole system, and describe the "bot wars" pattern.
5. Read the Bureau of Labor Statistics projections for three health-information
   jobs and explain why jobs that sit next to each other move in opposite
   directions.
6. Name the task in your intended specialty that a machine could most plausibly
   take over, estimate what fraction of the job it is, and say what would change
   your estimate.
7. Tell apart what AI *could* do in a job and what people are *seen* using it
   for. Look up a health job's score in one AI company's data and say what the
   score does not tell you.

Course competencies: AIM-7 (workflow and systems), AIM-2 (critical
appraisal), AIM-X (professional identity, the closing question).
:::

**What you need.** Your university ChatGPT Edu or Copilot account and a
browser. Nothing to install. Nothing in this chapter involves a patient. The
time counts about 22 minutes of reading, a 2-minute clip, about 38
minutes of doing, and a few minutes to check yourself. The longer video, the
"If you have more time" box, and Go deeper are optional.

## The year everyone says radiology is over

It is September of your fourth year. You have your radiology letters, your
program list, and a spreadsheet of interview dates. At a family dinner, an
uncle who reads about technology asks why you would go into the one specialty
the "godfather of AI" said should stop training people. He has the quote on
his phone. In 2016 Geoffrey Hinton told a Toronto audience that people should
*stop training radiologists now*. Within five years, he said, deep learning
would obviously do the job better. Hinton would later share a Nobel Prize for
the neural networks that make modern AI work.

::: {.vendor-slide}
<div class="brand">Machine Learning and the Market for Intelligence · Toronto · 2016</div>
<h4>"People should stop training radiologists now."</h4>
<div class="stats">
<div class="stat"><b>5 yrs</b><span>until deep learning "obviously" outperforms radiologists</span></div>
<div class="stat"><b>0</b><span>new radiologists needed</span></div>
</div>
<div class="foot">A confident forecast about a whole job, made by the person best placed to make it</div>
<div class="fine">Illustrative rendering of a public remark for this chapter; not the speaker's slide. The quote is real and is linked in the Watch section.</div>
:::

Your uncle is not wrong that Hinton said it. He is not wrong that Hinton knows
more about deep learning than anyone at the table. The question is what
happened next. Does the way the prediction failed tell you anything about the
job you are about to spend a decade training for? Not going into radiology?
The same uncle has a version of the question for every specialty, and so does
every chatbot. This chapter is about how to answer it with evidence.

## Why this matters

You are choosing a specialty for the next thirty years, mostly on instinct
and advice. Nobody can tell you how your specialty will look in 2056. But the most confident,
most credentialed prediction that a medical job would disappear has now had
its full time to come true. It failed in a specific way that you can learn from. A forecast
that has failed is more useful than one that has not been tested yet. You can
examine each assumption and see which ones were wrong.

There is a second reason, and your co-residents will not think of it. The
people whose jobs are already changing are not physicians. Medical
transcription is shrinking. Medical coding is growing. Both jobs are done close
to where you will work. A resident who understands why is more useful to the
team than one who is only relieved about their own position.

## How it works

### What actually happened

The prediction was five years. Ten years on, the National Resident Matching
Program's own tables show what happened in @fig-match. Diagnostic radiology offered
more advanced (PGY-2) positions in 2026 than in any of the previous four
years, and filled 98.4 percent of them. There were 1,741 applicants who ranked
the specialty for 1,083 positions.[^nrmp]

    on 2026-09-07. The figure shows advanced (PGY-2) diagnostic radiology
    positions; a further 156 categorical PGY-1 positions were offered in 2026
    and 148 filled.

The other workforce numbers agree. The Neiman Health Policy
Institute counted 37,482 radiologists serving Medicare patients in 2023. It
projected a workforce 25.7 percent larger by 2055 even if residency positions
stop growing, and 40.3 percent larger if they keep growing [@pmid:39952776].
Attrition, the rate at which working radiologists leave clinical practice,
more than doubled between 2014 and 2022, from 1.1 to 2.5 percent a year. The
authors treat that as one cause of a *shortage*, not a surplus
[@pmid:41031940].

In May 2025 Hinton told the *New York Times* that he had spoken too broadly in
2016. He said he had meant image analysis rather than the whole job. He now
expects most image interpretation to be done by "a combination of A.I. and a
radiologist."[^hinton] Here is the prediction as it was covered when it was
new, and as it reads now.

[^hinton]: Steve Lohr, "Your A.I. Radiologist Will Not Be With You Soon,"
    *New York Times*, 14 May 2025. The direct quotation is as reported by
    [AuntMinnie](https://www.auntminnie.com/imaging-informatics/artificial-intelligence/article/15746014/hinton-acknowledges-mistake-in-predicting-ai-replacement-of-radiologists),
    because the original is paywalled.

He Was Wrong.</a><div class="date">Arjun Byju, radiology resident · 25 October 2024</div></div>
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">The New York Times · technology</div><a class="hl" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/14/technology/ai-jobs-radiologists-mayo-clinic.html">Your A.I. Radiologist Will Not Be With You Soon</a><div class="date">Steve Lohr · 14 May 2025</div></div>
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">Radiology Business · trade press</div><a class="hl" href="https://radiologybusiness.com/topics/healthcare-management/healthcare-staffing/match-day-2026-radiology-programs-offer-more-positions-ever-applicant-pool-declines">Match Day 2026: Radiology programs offer more positions than ever, but applicant pool declines</a><div class="date">March 2026</div></div>
:::

Read the third clipping twice. "More positions than ever" and "applicant
pool declines" are in the same headline. The headline does not prove why the
pool shrank. But if students are hearing the prediction and acting on it, even
as the job market moves the other way, that is a harm the prediction did, and
the people who believed it were the ones harmed.

### Why "he was just early" is not enough

The easy explanation is that the prediction was only late. Hinton's own 2025 correction is
more interesting. He says he meant a task, image analysis, and said a job.
That is not a timing error. The most useful explanation of the failure has
four parts, each built into how medical work is organized. Each one is a
question you can ask about any specialty. The worksheets later in the chapter call them the four factors.

**1. Task decomposition: does the job break into tasks a machine can be tested
on?** A job can be automated only as far as it breaks into tasks a machine can
be measured on. In 2012, one trained observer followed fourteen staff
radiologists through their workdays at three hospitals, timing each
activity. The radiologists spent 36.4 percent of their time interpreting
images [@pmid:23763878].
The rest went to protocolling requests (deciding how each scan should be
done), supervising studies, procedures, talking with other physicians, and
direct patient care (@fig-workday). A tool that read every image perfectly
would leave nearly two-thirds of the day untouched. It would not sign the
report either.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-workday
%%| fig-alt: "Pie chart of a radiologist's day. Image interpretation 36.4 percent, clinical work other than reading images 43.8 percent, other clinical 7.5 percent, nonclinical 12.3 percent."
%%| fig-cap: "How fourteen hospital radiologists spent their time in 2012, from a time-and-motion study at three Vancouver hospitals. Redrawn from the abstract of Dhanoa et al. (2013): 36.4 percent image interpretation, 43.8 percent noninterpretive clinical tasks; the remaining categories are derived from the reported 87.7 percent total clinical productivity."
pie showData
    accTitle: How fourteen hospital radiologists spent their time in 2012, from a time-and-motion study at three Vancouver hospitals
    accDescr: Pie chart of a radiologist's day. Image interpretation 36.4 percent, clinical work other than reading images 43.8 percent, other clinical 7.5 percent, nonclinical 12.3 percent.
    title "A radiologist's day (percent of time)"
    "Image interpretation" : 36.4
    "Clinical work other than reading images" : 43.8

```

The same question has now been asked of emergency medicine. A team led by
Stanford emergency physicians combined six time-and-motion studies, the
national list of activities a resident must be trusted to do alone, and
O\*NET, the US government's list of the tasks in each job. That gave 14
categories of work. Then two emergency physicians on the team judged what
current AI could do with each. They placed AI replacement mainly in routine
record and office tasks: documentation, reviewing medical records, and
running the department's operations. Those tasks take 20 to 40 percent of a
shift. For the judgment-heavy work they judged that AI mostly helps rather
than replaces, and for hands-on work it does little [@pmid:42687470]. This
is expert judgment, not a measurement, but it is the same method: break the
job into tasks first.

**2. Generalization: does it work at a hospital that did not build it?** A
model that beats radiologists on a benchmark (a fixed test set) has beaten
them on one dataset. Deep-learning models for pneumonia on chest x-rays were
trained at one hospital system and tested at another. Performance dropped.
The models could also tell which hospital an image came from with better than
99.9 percent accuracy. They had learned the scanner as much as the disease
[@pmid:30399157].

**3. Liability: who signs, and who is blamed when it is wrong?** Someone signs
the read. Malpractice law judges the physician, not the model. The joint
statement of the American, Canadian, European, Australasian, and North
American radiology societies describes current tools as helping the
radiologist's interpretation, not replacing it. Tools that act on their own
are treated as a separate question needing their own evidence
[@pmid:38276923]. Where a device stops and who is liable when a tool is wrong
belong to [the ethics chapter](core-ethics-regulation.qmd). The point here is only that the
rules are built to keep a human involved in every decision, and rules change more slowly than
benchmarks.

**4. Demand: if the task gets cheaper, is more of it ordered?** Making a task
cheaper does not obviously reduce the number of people doing it. This is the
second of the course's four recurring lessons, **efficiency gains get eaten
by volume**; economists call it the Jevons paradox. In the nineteenth century, more efficient steam
engines led to more coal being burned, not less, because cheaper power got
used more. Imaging works the same way: cheaper scans get ordered more often.
The Neiman Health Policy Institute projects 17% to 27% more imaging in 2055
than in 2023, driven mostly by population growth and ageing, if per-person use
stays flat [@pmid:39952774]. Its companion paper projects the radiologist
workforce growing 26% to 40% over the same years [@pmid:39952776]. The
workforce projection above assumes demand keeps growing at least as fast as
supply.
The same paradox appears again in [the environmental-impact chapter](enrichment-environment.qmd), if you take
it. Efficiency per unit and total use move in opposite directions more often
than you would expect.

```{mermaid}

%%| fig-alt: "Flowchart. Pick one task in the job. Can a machine be measured on it? No: stays with the human. Yes: does it work at a hospital that did not build it? Not shown: stays with the human. Yes: who signs and who is liable when it is wrong? The physician: assists the human. The tool: is demand capped? No, more gets ordered: more of the task, same people. Yes: fewer people do this task."
%%| fig-cap: "The four questions, in the order they usually settle an argument. A task that fails any one of them stays with the human; a job is the sum of its tasks."

Yes, who signs and who is liable when it is wrong? The physician, assists the human. The tool, is demand capped? No, more gets ordered, more of the task, same people. Yes, fewer people do this task.
    T[Pick one task in the job] --> Q1{Can a machine be<br/>measured on it?}
```

Most physician jobs do not break neatly into tasks. The specialties that look most automatable from outside are the
ones whose pattern-recognition work is easiest to see, not the ones where it
is the largest share of the work.

### The precedent: mammography CAD

The closest earlier example went further than most students expect.
Computer-aided detection (CAD) for screening mammography is software that
marks suspicious spots on the image for the radiologist. The FDA approved it
in 1998. Medicare began paying extra for it in 2002. By the late 2000s it was
used on most screening mammograms in the United States, at a cost of over
$400 million a year [@pmid:26414882]. Measured by adoption, it was a success.

Then the outcome data arrived. Across 429,345 mammograms at 43 facilities,
adding CAD lowered specificity (the share of healthy women correctly called
normal) from 90.2 to 87.2 percent. It raised the biopsy rate by 19.7 percent.
It did not significantly change the cancer detection rate [@pmid:17409321]. A
later analysis of 625,625 digital mammograms found no improvement on any
measure with CAD. Among radiologists who read both with and without it,
sensitivity (the share of cancers found) was *lower* with CAD
[@pmid:26414882]. From January 2018 Medicare stopped paying separately for CAD. The new
mammography codes include CAD "when performed", so the add-on disappeared into
the base payment
([CMS Transmittal 3844, 2017](https://www.cms.gov/Regulations-and-Guidance/Guidance/Transmittals/2017Downloads/R3844CP.pdf)).
A technology was adopted at scale, generated extra procedures for patients,
and then disappeared once the payment stopped.

The finding to remember is smaller and worse. Readers were shown mammograms in
which an unusually high share of the CAD marks were wrong. Their sensitivity
fell compared with readers who had no computer output at all. It fell most on
exactly the cancers the computer had missed [@pmid:15354301]. The name for
this is automation bias: the habit of trusting a machine's suggestion more
than it deserves. It has been documented in aviation, in decision-support
software, and in imaging [@pmid:21685142]. CAD did not replace the
radiologists. It made some of them worse. That is a different and more
troubling failure than the one everyone was worried about. The same
thing happens with the sepsis alert you will silence in your first month. A tool that is
wrong in a systematic way makes the human worse rather than being corrected by
them. The defence is the same in both places: find out how often the tool is
wrong before you decide how much to trust it.

Adoption and outcomes are separate questions.

### The economics the debate leaves out

Everything so far points toward optimism about physician jobs. This section
complicates that, because "your job survives" and "the system gets better or
cheaper" are different claims.

**Within the organization.** Ambient scribes are software that listens to a
visit and drafts the note. At UCSF, a study followed 1,565 physicians and
about 1.2 million outpatient visits. Physicians who adopted a scribe billed
1.81 more relative value units (RVUs, the units Medicare uses to price
physician work) per week than those who did not. They saw 0.80 more patients
per week, with no rise in claim denials [@pmid:41511775]. This is an
association, not proof that the scribe caused the change; early adopters may
differ from other physicians. More billing is what a hospital's finance
office hopes for, and it is not cost reduction. It fits the same recurring
lesson: efficiency gains get eaten by volume.

**Across the system.** The Peterson Health Technology Institute takes no
vendor money. In March 2025 it concluded that scribes probably reduce burnout
but show little evidence of financial return. In April 2026 it concluded that
administrative AI reduces work *inside* organizations while failing to lower
system-wide costs, and possibly raising them.[^phti] The pattern it names is
"bot wars." Providers use AI to submit more prior-authorization requests (the
insurer's approval needed before a treatment) and to code visits at higher
levels. Payers use AI to process more denials and to "downcode" claims
automatically, paying at a lower level than billed. The number of
requests and denials rises, and no clinical question is settled any faster.

[^phti]: Peterson Health Technology Institute, *Adoption of AI in Healthcare
    Delivery Systems: Early Applications and Impacts* (March 2025) and
    *Administrative AI: Current Use and Potential Impact* (April 2026),
    <https://phti.org/administrative-ai-current-use-and-potential-impact/>.
    The "bot wars" phrase (Exhibit 4, on prior authorization) and the Level 5
    coding example (a 5% rise in Level 5 and 7% in Level 4 established-patient
    encounters after scribe deployment) are in the report PDF,
    <https://www.phti.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/PHTI-Administrative-AI-Current-Use-and-Potential-Impact.pdf>.

### The most useful single fact: the BLS contradiction

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) is the United States government agency
that publishes ten-year employment projections for every occupation, in its
*Occupational Outlook Handbook*. Three of those occupations sit side by side
in the medical records department (@fig-bls).

::: {#fig-bls}


Projected employment change, 2025 to 2035, for three health-information occupations. Redrawn from the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook pages for each occupation, read 2026-09-07. Same industry, same technology, opposite directions.

:::

| Occupation | 2025 jobs | Projected change, 2025–35 | BLS's stated reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Medical transcriptionists | 42,000 | −4% | Speech recognition and natural language processing let physicians document in real time |
| Medical records specialists | 200,700 | +8% | Aging population, chronic disease, more coding for reimbursement; AI coding tools "may affect" demand |
| Health information technologists and medical registrars | 42,000 | +16% | Growing volume of electronic health information needing analysis and registry maintenance |

: The three projections, with the reason BLS gives for each. Read from the *Occupational Outlook Handbook* on 2026-09-07: [transcriptionists](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/medical-transcriptionists.htm), [records specialists](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/medical-records-and-health-information-technicians.htm), [health information technologists](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/health-information-technologists-and-medical-registrars.htm). BLS revises these every two years. {#tbl-bls}

What separates them is the same four questions, applied to non-physician
work. Transcription is a single task a machine can be tested on. It works
anywhere, because speech is speech. Nobody signs a transcript. And its demand
is capped by the number of visits. Coding and health-information work pass
the first test only in part. Much of the job is judgment about what a record
means and what a payer will accept, and the bot wars above are *increasing* that work, not removing
it. The people whose jobs change first are your colleagues, and the harm is
not spread evenly. Transcription pays less than the two occupations that are
growing, so the displaced workers are the ones with the least money in reserve.
That is the course's fourth recurring lesson, **who benefits, who bears the
risk, who decides**, explained in [the ethics chapter](core-ethics-regulation.qmd). [The
bias and equity chapter](core-bias-equity.qmd) has a name for that, harms of allocation, and it
applies to jobs as much as to diagnosis.

### Could versus does: what one AI company sees

Everything so far asks whether a machine *could* do part of a job. In March
2026 Anthropic, the company that makes the Claude chatbot, published a
different number: what people were actually seen doing with Claude at
work.[^anthropic] The two authors, Maxim Massenkoff and Peter McCrory,
started from O\*NET, the government's list of job tasks. It lists about
18,000 tasks across about 800 occupations. For each
task they asked two questions.

- **Could a language model do it?** A language model is the kind of AI
  behind ChatGPT and Claude. An earlier study had rated every O\*NET task on
  whether a language model could do it at least twice as fast
  [@doi:10.1126/science.adj0998]. When it first appeared in 2023, three of
  its four authors were at OpenAI, the company that makes ChatGPT.
- **Was it seen being done?** The authors looked for the task in samples of
  people's work conversations with Claude, and in software that companies
  build on Claude, from August and November 2025. When Claude did the task
  on its own, the task counted in full. When Claude helped a person do it,
  the task counted half.

Each job then gets a score the authors call *observed exposure*. It is
roughly the share of the job's working time spent on tasks seen in that use.

[^anthropic]: Maxim Massenkoff and Peter McCrory, *Labor market impacts of
    AI: A new measure and early evidence*, Anthropic, 5 March 2026, corrected
    8 March 2026, <https://www.anthropic.com/research/labor-market-impacts>,
    read with its appendix on 2026-10-16. Published on the company's website,
    not in a peer-reviewed journal. The score for every occupation is in the
    Anthropic Economic Index dataset,
    <https://huggingface.co/datasets/Anthropic/EconomicIndex>, file
    `labor_market_impacts/job_exposure.csv`, released under CC BY.

![Could do versus does, for 22 job categories. Blue: the share of each category's tasks that a language model could do at least twice as fast, from the earlier study's ratings. Red: the share seen in work use of Claude in August and November 2025, with assisted use counted half. Redrawn from Massenkoff and McCrory (2026), Figure 2. The values were read from the published chart to about one percentage point ([the values as a table](../data/anthropic-labor-market-2026/figure2-radar-digitized.csv)). Data are not copyrightable; drawing by the course, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).](../images/anthropic-2026-could-vs-does.svg){#fig-could-does fig-alt="Radar chart with 22 job categories around a circle. A large blue shape shows the share of tasks a language model could do; a much smaller red shape inside it shows the share seen in work use of Claude. Red is largest for computer and math (about a third), office and admin, business and finance, and sales. Healthcare practitioners: could 60 percent, seen 5 percent. Healthcare support: could 28 percent, seen close to zero. Manual jobs such as construction and food service are low on both."}

The space between the two shapes in @fig-could-does is the paper's main
finding. In computer and math jobs, a language model could do about 94
percent of tasks, and about a third were seen. For healthcare
practitioners, the group that includes physicians, nurses, and pharmacists,
a model could do about 60 percent, and about 5 percent was seen.

The authors give a medical example of that gap. The earlier study rated
"Authorize drug refills and provide prescription information to pharmacies"
as a task a language model alone could make at least twice as fast.
Anthropic has not seen Claude
doing it. Among the reasons a possible task goes unused, the authors list
"legal constraints" and "human verification steps". For a refill, that is
the third of the four questions: someone signs the prescription, and the
law says who. A task can pass the first question and still stay with a
person.

The company released the score for every occupation (@fig-health-jobs).
Medical records specialists, the job that includes medical coders, scored
67 percent, the fourth highest of 756 jobs. Medical transcriptionists scored 64 percent. Radiologists, the
specialty Hinton said to stop training, scored 20 percent. Forty of the 65
jobs in the healthcare practitioner group scored zero, including family
medicine physicians and psychiatrists. A zero means Claude was not seen
doing enough of the job's tasks to count. It does not mean AI cannot help
with them.

![Observed exposure for selected health jobs: the share of each job's working time spent on tasks seen in work use of Claude, with assisted use counted half. The four records and office jobs are the highest-scoring health jobs in the data; the eight clinical jobs were chosen to show the range. Jobs that keep records score far higher than jobs that treat patients. Data: Anthropic Economic Index, `job_exposure.csv`, released with Massenkoff and McCrory (2026) under CC BY ([a copy in this book](../data/anthropic-labor-market-2026/job_exposure.csv)). Drawing by the course, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).](../images/anthropic-2026-health-jobs.svg){#fig-health-jobs fig-alt="Horizontal bar chart of observed exposure. For comparison, computer programmers score 75 percent, the highest of all 756 jobs. Records and office work: medical records specialists 67 percent, medical transcriptionists 64, medical secretaries and administrative assistants 36, health information technologists and registrars 31. Clinicians: radiologists 20, pathologists 16, nurse practitioners 9, pharmacists 9, general internal medicine physicians 8, registered nurses 6, family medicine physicians 0, psychiatrists 0."}

Now put these scores next to @tbl-bls. Medical records specialists and
medical transcriptionists are almost equally exposed. The BLS expects
records specialists to grow 8 percent and transcriptionists to shrink 4
percent. Exposure counts the tasks a tool touches. It does not tell you
whether the job will shrink. The four questions help you reason about
that. Transcription
demand is capped by the number of visits, and the bot wars are adding
coding work. Across all jobs, the paper found only a weak link with the BLS
projections. For every 10 percentage points more exposure, projected growth
to 2034 was 0.6 points lower.

People who know these jobs say the same. A University of Washington team
interviewed 14 people familiar with office work in allied health:
transcription, coding and billing, scheduling, and interpreting. They
concluded that "to date, most allied health workers' jobs with
administrative/management roles have not been at risk of replacement by
AI". They also heard that AI output has to be checked, and that checking
takes staff time. They warned that this could change: financial pressure on
health systems could push them to use AI in place of staff
[@pmid:42612020].

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="If you have more time: has AI cost jobs yet?"}
The Anthropic authors compared unemployment among the most
exposed quarter of workers with unemployment among workers whose jobs
scored zero. Since ChatGPT was released in November 2022, the gap between
the two groups has not changed by more than chance would explain. There is
one early sign. Workers aged 22 to 25 started new jobs in the most exposed
occupations about 14 percent less often than in 2022. Older workers showed
no such drop. The authors call the result "just barely
statistically significant". The young people who were not hired may have
stayed in other jobs or gone back to school. A Stanford team using payroll
records found a clearer drop. Its 2025 version ranked jobs by the earlier
study's "could" ratings, not by observed use. Through July 2025, employment of
workers aged 22 to 25 in the most exposed jobs fell 13 percent compared
with other workers.[^canaries] In the authors' August 2026 update, with data
through June 2026, the gap was 19 percent. It shrinks when the workers'
education is taken into account, and it is smaller in national survey data.
The 2025 paper found the opposite for health aides
(nursing, psychiatric, and home health aides), which sit in the least
exposed fifth of jobs. Employment of young health aides grew faster than
that of older ones. The paper does not test why. One reading is the fourth
question: demand for hands-on care keeps growing, and a language model
cannot do that work. Residency positions are not what these studies
measure. The young workers in them are more like the coders, scribes, and
unit clerks you will work beside.
:::

[^canaries]: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, and Ruyu Chen, *Canaries in
    the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of
    Artificial Intelligence*, Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper, 26
    August 2025, read from the
    [archived August 2025 version](https://web.archive.org/web/20250901000000id_/https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Canaries_BrynjolfssonChandarChen.pdf)
    on 2026-10-16; the health-aide finding is on page 11. The payroll data
    come from ADP, a payroll company. The August 2026 revision, at the
    [same address](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Canaries_BrynjolfssonChandarChen.pdf),
    gives the 19 percent figure in its abstract and moves the health-aide
    panel to appendix Figure B.5. It also notes that ADP's data hold fewer
    health, education, and government workers than the national figures. Quote
    the version you read, with its date.

**Read it as you would read a trial run by the company that sells the
drug.** Five things to notice.

1. The authors work for the company whose product they measured. Both of
   the paper's main findings, wide use of the product and no rise in
   unemployment so far, are ones the company would welcome.
2. It is one product. A clinician who uses ChatGPT, or a scribe built on
   another company's model, does not appear in Claude's data.
3. It is a company report, not a peer-reviewed paper.
4. The authors warn that O\*NET can word the same activity differently for
   different jobs, and that this changes the score. So do not read much into
   small differences between specialties, such as 8 percent for general
   internal medicine and 0 for family medicine.
5. This section, like most of this book, was drafted with Claude.
   [The AI ledger](../appendix/ai-ledger.qmd) records what a person checked.

On the other side, the authors published their method, the judgment calls
they made, and the scores, so anyone can read the scores and see how they
were made. You will look some up in Part C.

## Watch or listen

**First, the source (1 min 24 s).** "Geoff Hinton: On Radiology," Creative
Destruction Lab, YouTube, uploaded 24 November 2016.
<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2HMPRXstSvQ>. Watch it before reading anything about it. Notice how
specific the claim is, how confident the tone is, and that the whole argument
is about image analysis. He is describing a task and forecasting a job. That
difference is what this chapter is about.

**Then, if you have time, the other side (optional; the first 20
minutes).** "AIMI Grand Rounds:
Developing Clinically Useful AI for Radiology," Curtis Langlotz, Stanford AIMI,
YouTube, 30 January 2025, 59 min 37 s.
<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WS9p0wFw7uY>. Langlotz is the radiologist
who wrote, in 2019, that AI will not replace radiologists, but radiologists
who use AI will replace those who do not [@pmid:33937794]. Listen for what he
says makes a tool *clinically useful*, as opposed to merely accurate. Listen
also for every place where the obstacle he describes is one of the four
questions rather than model performance. Twenty minutes is enough for the
exercise. The rest is worth hearing when you have time.

If you would rather read than watch, Deena Mousa's essay, listed under Go
deeper, covers the same material in about the same time.

## Do

Made-up patients only. [What counts as patient
information](../course/patient-information.qmd).

### Part A: ask the four questions with ChatGPT (15 minutes)

**Step 1. Ask.** Open ChatGPT Edu (Copilot also works) and paste this,
with your intended specialty in place of `<specialty>` (or radiology if you
are undecided):

```
I am a fourth-year medical student going into <specialty>. Use these
four questions to think about how AI may change the job by 2036:
1. Does the job break into tasks a machine can be tested on? Which ones?
2. Do tools for those tasks work at hospitals that did not build them?
3. Who signs the result, and who is liable when it is wrong?
4. If the task gets cheaper, will more of it be ordered?
Then search for two or three published studies of how <specialty>
physicians spend their working day (time-and-motion studies) or of the
<specialty> workforce. For each, give the authors, journal, year, a link,
and the number I should look for.
```

**Step 2. Record what it said.** One line per question, and whether it gave
you something you can check: a number, a study, a link.

```
Tool: ____________________   Specialty: ____________________

Question          What it said (one line)                Checkable?
Tasks             ____________________________________   Y / N
Generalization    ____________________________________   Y / N
Liability         ____________________________________   Y / N
Demand            ____________________________________   Y / N
```

**Step 3. Check one study.** Ask, then check: most of a good answer is
right, and your job is to find out which parts. Pick the study the answer
leans on most. Open the link, or search its title in PubMed. Does the paper
exist, and does its abstract contain the number the answer gave?

```
The study I checked: ________________________________  PMID: __________
It exists: Y / N     It contains the number: Y / N
What I found: _________________________________________________________
```

It may get this right. If so, you know because you found the number in the
abstract yourself. If it got the study or the number wrong, tell it what you
found and ask again. Either way, note which parts of the answer held up.

### Part B: your own forecast (12 minutes)

**Step 1. Find out how the time is actually spent.** The 36 percent figure for
radiology came from someone with a stopwatch. Most specialties have such a
study. Use the one you checked in Part A if it held up. If not, search
PubMed with:

```
"time and motion studies"[MeSH] AND <your specialty>
```

adding `physician` or `resident` if the results are mostly about nurses.
Read the abstracts of the two most recent studies that observed physicians
rather than surveying them. Going into emergency medicine? Start with the
paper under question 1 [@pmid:42687470], which already combines six such
studies. Write down how the day divides. If your specialty
has no such study, say so on the sheet. That absence is itself a finding about
how well the job is understood. In that case, use your own sub-internship,
labeled honestly as one observer's estimate.

**Step 2. Write three lines.**

```
Specialty: ____________________

1. The most automatable TASK in this specialty (a task, not the job):
   __________________________________________________________________

2. What fraction of the working day that task is, and where the number
   comes from (study / my own estimate):
   ______ %   source: ____________________________________________

3. The factor most likely to make my estimate wrong, and why:
   [ ] task decomposition  [ ] generalization  [ ] liability  [ ] demand
   __________________________________________________________________
```

Radiology's 36 percent is the number to compare yours against. Most students
overestimate the fraction for their own field when they first write it down.
That is fine. The point of writing it down is to have a number you can check
later.

**Step 3. Argue against it.** Reread your line 2 as the uncle at dinner. What
would he say is missing? Then reread it as the radiology resident who wrote
the first press clipping. Change the number if either of them convinced you,
and say which.

### Part C: check the numbers yourself (11 minutes)

The BLS projections change every two years. Read them from the source.

**Step 1.** Open the three BLS pages linked under @tbl-bls in your browser.
For each, find the "Job Outlook" section and record:

```
Occupation                          Projected change   Decade     BLS's stated reason
Medical transcriptionists           ______ %           ____–____  ___________________
Medical records specialists         ______ %           ____–____  ___________________
Health information technologists    ______ %           ____–____  ___________________
```

If your numbers differ from @tbl-bls, BLS has revised the projections since
this chapter was written. Note the new decade, and trust the page over the
chapter.

**Step 2. Look up how exposed each job is.** The table below holds the
observed exposure score for all 756 occupations in Anthropic's data. It
loads in your browser from the file the company released. Type part of a
job title to filter it, and record the scores for the same three
occupations.

```
Occupation                          Observed exposure
Medical transcriptionists           ______ %
Medical records specialists         ______ %
Health information technologists    ______ %
```

Then look up the job closest to the specialty you are entering. Some
specialties have no row, including emergency medicine, general surgery, and
cardiology. Use the nearest job, such as "Physicians, All Other", and say
which you used. If it scores zero, write one line on what that zero does and
does not mean.

::: {.widget}
```{ojs}
exposureJobs = FileAttachment("../data/anthropic-labor-market-2026/job_exposure.csv").csv({ typed: true })
viewof exposureQuery = Inputs.search(exposureJobs, {
  columns: ["title"],
  label: "Find a job",
  placeholder: "Type part of a job title, for example nurse"
})
Inputs.table(exposureQuery, {
  // Score first, so a narrow screen cuts off long job titles, not the score.
  columns: ["observed_exposure", "title"],
  header: { observed_exposure: "Exposure", title: "Occupation" },
  format: { observed_exposure: d => `${Math.round(d * 100)}%` },
  width: { observed_exposure: 90 },
  align: { observed_exposure: "right" },
  sort: "observed_exposure",
  reverse: true,
  rows: 10
})
```
:::

If the table does not load, open
[the file](../data/anthropic-labor-market-2026/job_exposure.csv) in your
browser. The table shows Anthropic's March 2026 release; the company says it
will update the scores.

**Step 3.** In two sentences, explain why the first occupation moves one way
and the other two move the other way. Two of the three scored almost the
same in Step 2, so exposure alone cannot be the reason. Use at least two of the four questions by name.
Then one more sentence: who bears the cost of the −4 percent, and what does
that group look like compared with the +16 percent one?

## Check

Score yourself against this before moving on. Objective numbers refer to the
list at the top of the chapter.

| You have | Meets | Falls short |
|---|---|---|
| The prediction and its outcome (obj. 1) | You can state the 2016 claim, give two primary numbers from 2026 (positions, fill rate, or workforce projection), and say in one sentence why "early" is the wrong diagnosis | "He was wrong" with no number, or "he was just early" |
| The four questions for your specialty (obj. 2) | All four rows filled, and one study opened and checked against the number the answer gave | Rows filled without checking anything |
| Your three-line forecast (obj. 2, 6) | A task, not a job; a fraction with a named source or an honest "my estimate"; a factor with a reason | "Documentation, 50%, probably fine" |
| The CAD sentence (obj. 3) | "Adoption and outcomes are separate questions," with the biopsy-rate finding attached | Only the slogan |
| The system-cost sentence (obj. 4) | You can explain in your own words why 1.81 more RVUs a week is not a cost reduction, and what "bot wars" means | "AI saves money" or "AI wastes money" without a mechanism |
| Three BLS rows (obj. 5) | Numbers and reasons read from the live pages, and a two-sentence explanation that names two factors | Numbers copied from this chapter |
| Could versus does (obj. 7) | You can say what the blue and red shapes in @fig-could-does measure, give the two healthcare-practitioner numbers, and explain why two almost equally exposed jobs have opposite BLS projections. For your own job's score, you can say what it does not tell you | "Medical coders will be replaced," from the 67 percent alone |

## What this changes for you

*What does this change about how you'll practice, and what would you have to
see in the next five years to conclude you got this wrong?*

Write both halves down. For the first, go back to the dinner table. Your uncle
is still holding his phone. What do you say about the 2016 quote, using one
number from this chapter and one of the four questions? If you are not going
into radiology, answer for your own specialty, with your Part B line 2 as the
number. For the second half, name the observation that would make you change
your forecast: a match statistic, a workforce projection, a BLS revision, a
change in who signs the report. A forecast that nothing could prove wrong is
not a forecast.

Then keep the sheet from Part B. Reread it at the end of residency. Every
student who does this exercise has just made a confident forecast about a
medical specialty. So did a Nobel laureate, with better information than any
of you, and he got the mechanism wrong. The point of writing it down is to be
able to check.

Your forecast, and what would change it, can go into your week 4 piece,
"what you will keep" (see the [learning journal](../course/learning-journal.qmd)).

## Go deeper

### More numbers behind the story

Optional. These were in the main text and were moved here to keep it short.

**Radiology pay.** Doximity's 2026 pay survey put average diagnostic
radiology pay at $609,684 for 2025, up 6.6 percent in a year when physician
pay overall rose about 2 percent ([Doximity, *2026 Physician Compensation
Report*](https://www.doximity.com/reports/physician-compensation-report/2026)).
The previous year's report gave $571,749, up 7.5 percent. These are
different survey years, not competing estimates, so quote one with its year.

**The subspecialty exception.** Count the radiologists who bill at least half
their work for children. That pediatric radiology workforce shrank from 2,190
in 2016 to 2,032 in 2023, from 6.4 to 4.6 percent of all radiologists, while
demand for imaging rose [@pmid:40923948]. That is not automation. It is the
job market of one subspecialty moving on its own, apart from its parent
specialty. A student choosing a fellowship is making a more specific
decision than the overall numbers describe.

**FDA devices.** Radiology has most of the FDA-authorized AI devices. An
analysis of the 903 AI-enabled devices the FDA had authorized by August 2024
found that 692 (76.6 percent) were radiology devices. It found a clinical
performance study reported for about half of all 903 [@pmid:40305017]. There
are hundreds of cleared radiology tools, and so far no measured loss of
radiologist jobs. The most widely read explanation of why is Deena Mousa's
essay ["AI isn't replacing radiologists"](https://www.understandingai.org/p/ai-isnt-replacing-radiologists)
(*Understanding AI*, 1 October 2025). She also reports that 38 percent of
models cleared in 2024 that disclosed their test sites used data from a
single hospital. That figure is her reading of the same analysis; it is not
in the paper's main text
[VERIFY: not in the main text of pmid:40305017, checked 2026-09-08; the site counts would be in Supplement 1, which a person should open]{.verify}.

**Scribes across five health systems.** A study followed 8,581 clinicians at
five academic health systems, 1,809 of whom adopted a scribe. Adoption was
associated with modestly less time in the EHR and on documentation, and
slightly more visits each week [@pmid:41920565]. The Peterson Health
Technology Institute's April 2026 report also records a health system where
Level 5 visit coding (the highest billing level for an office visit) rose 5
percent after scribes arrived, worth over $1,000 per provider per month.
That is the UCSF finding seen from the payer's side.

**Percent of what?** You will hear that "25 percent of health care spending
is administrative." That sentence blends three studies with three different
denominators, that is, three different answers to "percent of what?" Shrank
and colleagues estimated total *waste* at $760 to $935 billion, about 25
percent of spending. Administrative complexity is one of six categories of
that waste [@pmid:31589283]. Himmelstein and colleagues found administration
to be 25.3 percent of *hospital* spending, the highest of eight countries
[@pmid:25201663]. Woolhandler and colleagues put administration at $294.3
billion in 1999, 31.0 percent of spending *after exclusions*, using the
broadest definition in the literature [@pmid:12930930]. Asking "percent of
what?" will stay useful after all three figures are out of date. Test
yourself: can you name the three denominators?

**What other companies' data show.** A Microsoft team scored how much AI
could help with each job, from about 200,000 conversations with Microsoft's
own Bing Copilot chatbot in 2024. Of 22 job groups, healthcare support
scored lowest, 0.05 on a scale from 0 to 1, and healthcare practitioners
scored 0.12.[^copilot] An Ohio State team reanalysed Anthropic's earlier
public data, more than 4 million Claude conversations from December 2024
and January 2025. Tasks from health practitioner jobs made up 2.58 percent
of conversations, against 37.22 percent for computing. The data could not
tell a clinician from a patient asking about their own care
[@pmid:40446149].

[^copilot]: Kiran Tomlinson, Sonia Jaffe, Will Wang, Scott Counts, and
    Siddharth Suri, *Working with AI: Measuring the Applicability of
    Generative AI to Occupations*, arXiv:2507.07935, version 6, 22 December
    2025, Table S2, <https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07935>. All five authors work
    at Microsoft.

**The measures disagree.** Medical transcriptionists score 64 percent in
Anthropic's data and 0.08 in Microsoft's. In the OpenAI-led study, its
language model rated transcriptionists 0.88 on the study's main exposure
scale, and its human raters rated them 0.23 (both from the study's data
file, listed below). Each number answers a different question, on a
different scale, made by a different group. Ask which measure it is, and
who made it, before you quote one.

**More coverage of the prediction.**

::: {.press-clips}
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">The New Yorker · magazine</div><a class="hl" href="https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2017/04/03/ai-versus-md">A.I. Versus M.D.: What happens when diagnosis is automated?</a><div class="date">Siddhartha Mukherjee · 3 April 2017</div></div>
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">Fortune · business</div><a class="hl" href="https://fortune.com/article/ai-godfather-radiologists-obsolete-salaries-up-to-571k-demand-growing/">A decade after the 'Godfather of AI' said radiologists were obsolete, their salaries are up to $571K and demand is growing fast</a><div class="date">2026</div></div>
:::

### Data you can use yourself

Each of these opens in a browser and is free. The licence is as stated on
each page.

- **Anthropic's occupation scores**, the file behind @fig-health-jobs and
  the Part C table: one row per occupation, observed exposure from 0 to 1.
  On [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Anthropic/EconomicIndex),
  file `labor_market_impacts/job_exposure.csv`, CC BY; also
  [a copy in this book](../data/anthropic-labor-market-2026/job_exposure.csv).
  The values behind @fig-could-does, read from the paper's chart, are
  [a separate table](../data/anthropic-labor-market-2026/figure2-radar-digitized.csv).
- **The "could" ratings** from the OpenAI-led study, for every task and
  every occupation, with the language model's and the human raters' scores
  side by side. On [GitHub](https://github.com/openai/GPTs-are-GPTs), file
  `data/occ_level.csv`, MIT licence.
- **Microsoft's applicability scores**, one row per occupation, 785 in all.
  On [GitHub](https://github.com/microsoft/working-with-ai), file
  `ai_applicability_scores.csv`, CC BY 4.0.
- **O\*NET**, the task lists all of these studies start from. Search for a
  job at [O\*NET OnLine](https://www.onetonline.org/) to read its tasks; the
  [full database](https://www.onetcenter.org/database.html) downloads as CSV
  files, CC BY 4.0.
- **BLS projections** for every occupation, ten years ahead, in
  [one table](https://www.bls.gov/emp/tables/occupational-projections-and-characteristics.htm).
  US government work, public domain.
- **The Stanford team's monthly tracker**, which keeps the employment-by-age
  series of the payroll study up to date, with a separate file for home
  health aides: the [Canaries dashboard](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/project/indicators/canaries-dashboard/).
  No licence stated.

### Papers

- The time-and-motion study behind the 36 percent [@pmid:23763878], and the
  editorial that gave the field its slogan [@pmid:33937794].
- The two CAD studies [@pmid:17409321; @pmid:26414882] and the automation-bias
  experiment [@pmid:15354301], read together as one story.
- The generalization paper [@pmid:30399157], which is short and has a figure
  you will remember.
- The Neiman workforce papers: supply through 2055 [@pmid:39952776], attrition
  [@pmid:41031940], and the pediatric subspecialty [@pmid:40923948].
- The multi-society statement on buying and monitoring radiology AI
  [@pmid:38276923], which is what a department actually does with a cleared
  tool.
- The scribe economics: the five-system study [@pmid:41920565] and the UCSF
  productivity analysis [@pmid:41511775]. The five-system study is also in
  [the appraisal chapter](core-appraisal.qmd).
- The three administrative-cost papers [@pmid:31589283; @pmid:25201663;
  @pmid:12930930], for the denominators.
- Could versus does: the task ratings behind "could"
  [@doi:10.1126/science.adj0998], the emergency medicine task analysis
  [@pmid:42687470], the allied health interviews [@pmid:42612020], and the
  reanalysis of Claude conversations in health jobs [@pmid:40446149].

### Readings and talks

- Deena Mousa, ["AI isn't replacing radiologists"](https://www.understandingai.org/p/ai-isnt-replacing-radiologists)
  (October 2025). The four questions in this chapter are a short version of
  her argument.
- Peterson Health Technology Institute, [*Administrative AI: Current Use and
  Potential Impact*](https://phti.org/administrative-ai-current-use-and-potential-impact/)
  (April 2026), and KFF's interview with its director,
  ["The AI Arms Race in Administrative Health Care"](https://www.kff.org/other-health/the-ai-arms-race-in-administrative-health-care/)
  (July 2026).
- Maxim Massenkoff and Peter McCrory,
  [*Labor market impacts of AI*](https://www.anthropic.com/research/labor-market-impacts)
  (Anthropic, March 2026). Short and readable. Its appendix lists the
  judgment calls the authors made.
- [A history of AI in medicine](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2025-09-30-ai-history/)
  tells the IBM Watson story, from Jeopardy! to MD Anderson setting it aside
  in 2017, and covers MYCIN and the AI winters before it. Read it if you want
  a second example of the same shape before deciding the Hinton story is about
  one man's bad call. Also in [the foundations chapter](core-foundations.qmd).
- [AI and machine learning for an oncology service line](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-10-28-ai-ml-oncology-service-line/)
  keeps apart the four groups the economics section needs to keep apart:
  patients, providers, researchers, and administrators. It also lists eight
  guiding principles [@doi:10.1038/s43856-023-00279-9]. Two of them, "have
  high healthcare value" and "reduce overdiagnosis and overtreatment," are
  the CAD story stated as rules. The deck is also in [the ethics chapter](core-ethics-regulation.qmd); the
  principles are also in [the appraisal chapter](core-appraisal.qmd).
